subtype: Approach: working backward from the fair date [Thinking]
passage: Maria pressed her thumb on the calendar in the hall. The science fair was on the twenty-fourth, exactly three weeks away. "Last week is for the display board," she muttered, and drew a box round the final seven days. "Middle week is the experiment. So the first week is..." She counted backwards with her pencil, stopped at a Monday and tapped it. "Start here. Not later." Her friend Shreya leaned over from the sofa. "You haven't even picked what to grow yet." "That's the Monday job," Maria said, and wrote CHOOSE PLANT in the first box. Her shoulders felt a little lighter.

qa.q: How many weeks were there until the science fair?
qa.a: There were three weeks until the science fair.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling as she wrote CHOOSE PLANT in the first box?
qa.a: A little relieved, because the plan gave her a clear place to begin; the passage says her shoulders felt lighter.

qa.q: What other approach could Maria use if she is unsure the experiment fits in one week, and why?
qa.a: She could list each step of the experiment and guess how long each takes, so the middle week is based on real needs rather than a round number.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Maria's plan?
qa.a: Shreya seems to find it early, since no plant is chosen yet, but Maria has already given that a slot on the first Monday. 🙂

grounding: A girl plans a science fair project by fixing the end date first and placing each stage before it.

subtype: Approach: writing observations in a daily notebook [Action]
passage: Every morning before brushing his teeth, Devang carried a steel ruler to the balcony. He held it beside the bean plant, read the number, and wrote it in a green notebook under the date: 3 June, 4 cm. On the ninth day his sister Dilnaz peered over his shoulder. "You're only writing numbers." "That's the point," Devang said. "See, a tiny change on day five, then a big jump." Three weeks later he copied the dates and heights onto chart paper. The line climbed slowly with one flat stretch, but every dot on it was something he had really measured.

qa.q: What did Devang write in his green notebook each morning?
qa.a: He wrote the plant's height under the date.

qa.q: What does Devang's reply to Dilnaz suggest about how he feels about the daily notes?
qa.a: He feels quietly proud and sure that the plain numbers matter, because he points to the jump they reveal.

qa.q: What could Devang add to his notebook habit in case he misses a morning, and why?
qa.a: He could take a photo of the plant beside the ruler each day, so a missing note can be checked against a picture.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see the notebook at first?
qa.a: She sees only a list of numbers, as her remark shows, and has not yet noticed the jump that Devang can point to.

grounding: A boy measures a plant every morning and dates each note, so his final chart holds real numbers.

subtype: Approach: getting a parent to do the main work [Pitfall]
passage: The school hall smelled of chart paper and glue. Pema's water pump stood on the table, neat and shining, with a typed report beside it. Papa had built it over two evenings and typed the report himself. Ms Disha, the judge, stopped in front of it. "How does the water move up the pipe, Pema?" He glanced at the pump. "Um... Papa put the valve here. I think it goes... in." His ears turned hot. "Which part did you make yourself?" "Colouring the label." She smiled gently, wrote something on her sheet and moved on. Pema stared at the pipe. He could not have explained a single part.

qa.q: Which part of the project did Pema make himself?
qa.a: Pema said he made only the label, by colouring the label.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when the judge asked how the water moves up the pipe?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a little ashamed, since his ears turned hot and he could not explain his own model.

qa.q: What could Pema and his father do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Pema could build the parts himself while his father only checks and answers questions, so Pema would understand the pump and could explain it.

qa.q: How might Ms Disha see the model and Pema's answers together?
qa.a: She sees a polished model but a boy who cannot say how it works, which suggests someone else did most of the work, and she responds kindly.

grounding: A boy hands the main work to his father, so the project looks fine but he cannot explain it and learns little.

subtype: Approach: repeating the experiment when the result looks odd [Revision]
passage: In the kitchen of her flat in Bergen, Astrid measured the two bean plants again. The one in the cupboard was taller than the one on the windowsill, which made no sense for a plant in the dark. "Maybe the seeds were just different," said Bao, her classmate. Astrid frowned at the cupboard. The door stood open a hand's width, and a strip of light fell across the pot. "That's not dark." She shut it and wedged it with a book, then planted a fresh seed and marked the date. Ten days later the plant behind the closed door was thin and pale, and Astrid wrote the new numbers beside the crossed-out first ones.

qa.q: Where was the plant that grew taller than expected?
qa.a: It was in the cupboard.

qa.q: What was going through Astrid's mind when she saw the strip of light on the pot?
qa.a: She realised the test was not truly dark, so the odd result could not be trusted; she felt a jolt of surprise and then determination.

qa.q: What other approach could Astrid use to make sure the next test is fair?
qa.a: She could set up two matching pots at once, one in a closed box and one by the window, and check the box each time so no light gets in.

qa.q: How might Bao see Astrid's decision to repeat the test?
qa.a: Bao first guessed the seeds were different, so the repeat may look like extra work, but the new result shows the open door mattered.

grounding: A girl gets an odd result, finds the cause, repeats the test with the door shut and gets a clearer result.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing how to explain the project to visitors [Action]
passage: Thursday night. Fair is on Saturday! Today I practised my one-minute talk in front of the mirror: what I asked (does a plant lean toward light?), what I did (bean plant by the window, box turned each day), what I found (it bent toward the glass in four days). 58 seconds. Then I made my sister Leela sit on the bed and fire the hardest questions she could think of. She asked, "Why didn't you use two plants?" and I froze for a whole breath. Now the answer is on a card. Leela was a pretty good judge and I told her so. 🙂 Tomorrow, once more with the card. - Nikhil

qa.q: How long did Nikhil's practice talk take?
qa.a: It took 58 seconds.

qa.q: How did Nikhil feel when Leela asked why Nikhil had not used two plants?
qa.a: Caught off guard and briefly worried; freezing for a whole breath shows the question was a surprise.

qa.q: What other way could Nikhil prepare for tricky questions, and why?
qa.a: Nikhil could ask a classmate to question the project too, since a different person may ask something Leela did not think of.

qa.q: What might Leela feel about her part in the practice?
qa.a: Leela probably enjoys playing the judge and is pleased that Nikhil praised the questions, since Nikhil told her she was good at it.

grounding: A child rehearses a one-minute talk of the question, method and finding, with a sister asking hard questions.

subtype: Approach: presenting an unexpected result honestly [Revision]
passage: Sit, beta. Your grandmother Reena has a story about a bean plant. When I was ten, we grew beans for the school fair. I put one pot in the dark cupboard and wrote on my paper that it would stay green. It grew, but pale as chalk. My classmate Ganga whispered, "Change it, write green." I nearly did. Then I thought, the plant did not lie, so why should I? At the fair I stood by my board and said, "I guessed green, and it turned pale, and that surprised me." The old teacher judging asked why. I said I did not know yet. He gave me a ribbon, but I remember his smile more.

qa.q: What colour was the plant that grew in the cupboard?
qa.a: It was pale as chalk.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when Ganga whispered to change the paper?
qa.a: She felt tempted and uneasy, since she nearly did it and then reasoned that the plant had not lied.

qa.q: What choice did young Reena make at the fair, and why did it work out?
qa.a: She chose to show the pale plant and say she was surprised, and the judge valued her honesty enough to give her a ribbon.

qa.q: How did the judging teacher see Reena's answer that she did not know yet?
qa.a: The teacher seems to have taken it as honest work, giving her a ribbon and a smile.

grounding: A child keeps her unexpected pale-plant result and explains her surprise instead of changing the results.

subtype: Approach: getting used to water in the shallow end first [Thinking]
passage: Every Saturday I watch the new boy in our swim class, Uday, stand at the pool's edge with his arms folded. Today he stepped down to where the water reached only his knees and stayed there, splashing a little with one hand. I heard him mutter, "If I'm okay here, maybe up to my waist. If that's okay, then floating." He said it like a list. His face looked stiff, maybe scared, maybe just cold, I can't tell. After ten minutes he splashed with both hands and even laughed, once, quickly. The coach didn't push him. I told him "nice" and he nodded without looking at me. - Tenzin

qa.q: How deep was the water where Uday stood first?
qa.a: It reached only his knees.

qa.q: What does Uday's muttered list suggest about how he is handling his fear?
qa.a: It suggests he calms himself by taking one small step at a time and feeling safe before moving on, though his stiff face shows some fear stayed.

qa.q: What other approach could help Uday reach the floating step, and why?
qa.a: He could practise floating while the coach stands close and steadies him, so the next step comes with help and grows gradually.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Uday's start?
qa.a: Tenzin cannot tell whether the stiff face meant fear or cold, but notices the laugh and stays quiet, seeing a slow, brave beginning.

grounding: A boy afraid of water starts in the shallow end and reasons that feeling safe there leads to the next step.

subtype: Approach: following the coach's step-by-step drills [Action]
passage: Sunday. Three steps at swim class today. First I held the side and kicked until my legs felt like jelly. Then bubbles: face in, blow out slowly through my mouth, again and again. Then Coach Preeti gave me a foam noodle and I floated on my back for a few whole seconds! Coach says one little thing at a time, so it never felt like too much. Next week she wants me to let go of the side. My tummy did a flip when she said that, but a good flip, I think. 🙂 - Chandrika

qa.q: What did Chandrika do first in the lesson?
qa.a: Chandrika held the side and kicked.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel when Coach Preeti mentioned letting go of the side?
qa.a: A mix of nervous and excited, since Chandrika's tummy did a flip that seemed like a good one.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do if letting go still feels too big, and why?
qa.a: Chandrika could let go for just a moment with the coach close by, then a little longer, so the step gets even smaller.

qa.q: Why might Coach Preeti keep each step so small?
qa.a: Coach Preeti wants Chandrika to feel able rather than overwhelmed, so each step builds on the last.

grounding: A learner follows a coach's small drills in order: kicking at the side, bubbles, then floating with a noodle.

subtype: Approach: jumping into the deep end to prove he is brave [Pitfall]
passage: At the municipal pool in Valencia, Yosef watched Santiago and two others dare each other at the edge. "Bet you won't jump in the deep end," Santiago said. The coach had gone inside for a whistle. Yosef, who could only manage the shallow lanes, took a breath and jumped. The cold closed over his head. He kicked, swallowed a mouthful of water and could not find the bottom. Santiago shouted for help. The lifeguard dived in and hauled him to the wall while he coughed. Later, wrapped in a towel, Yosef listened as the coach spoke to the whole group. His legs still shook. He had wanted to look brave; now he only wanted to learn properly.

qa.q: Where did Yosef jump?
qa.a: He jumped into the deep end of the pool.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling as he sat wrapped in the towel?
qa.a: Shaky and scared, and a little ashamed, since he wanted to look brave but now only wants to learn properly.

qa.q: What could Yosef have done when Santiago dared him?
qa.a: He could have said no and asked the coach for a lesson, because being brave can mean choosing to learn safely.

qa.q: How might the lifeguard see what happened?
qa.a: The lifeguard sees a child in trouble in water too deep for his skill and acts at once, so the focus is on getting him out safely.

grounding: A boy jumps into the deep pool without the coach to prove he is brave, panics, is pulled out and learns skill matters.

subtype: Approach: noticing she is tense and relaxing her body [Revision]
passage: Each time Bindu lay back in the village tank at Sonpur, her heels dropped and her nose filled with water. "Again," called Naveen Sir from the steps. The third time she came up coughing. He crouched at the edge. "Bindu, your arms are like two sticks. Your whole back is tight." She looked at her hands; the fingers were spread and stiff. She took a slow breath, let her shoulders fall and opened her arms wide like a fan. Her ears slipped under, the sky filled her eyes, and for the first time the water held her up. She heard herself laugh.

qa.q: Who told Bindu her arms and back were tight?
qa.a: Naveen Sir told her.

qa.q: What did Bindu feel when the water finally held her up?
qa.a: She felt surprised and delighted, since she heard herself laugh.

qa.q: What other approach could help Bindu if she tenses up again, and why?
qa.a: She could take a few slow breaths before each try, or float with the coach's hand under her back, so she relaxes before the water holds her.

qa.q: How does Naveen Sir see Bindu's sinking?
qa.a: He sees stiffness rather than lack of ability, so he names it plainly and lets her fix it herself.

grounding: A child sinks while floating until the coach points out her stiffness and she relaxes and lets the water hold her.
